kf1.tip: Argue for and against: William Cecil, Principal Secretary then Lord Treasurer 1558-1598, was the minister Elizabeth could not do without. Then decide.
kf1.note: A strong answer weighs Cecil's forty years of service, his patient memoranda turning decisions into working policy, and the smooth handover to Robert. Against him, Walsingham uncovered the Babington Plot, and the Council advised while the queen decided. Most conclude Cecil was the hardest to replace, because he kept the whole machine running. The trap is treating Cecil as the one who made policy, when Elizabeth kept the final say.

kf2.tip: Rank Cecil, Walsingham and the Privy Council by how much each kept Elizabeth safe on her throne, and defend each place in one line.
kf2.note: A strong answer weighs direct threats stopped, the daily running of the kingdom, and who held real power. Many put Walsingham first, because his spies exposed the Babington Plot and removed Mary, Queen of Scots. Cecil comes next for finance, stability and long service. The Council comes last, since it only advised and passed on orders. The trap is ranking by fame alone, or mixing up Mary, Queen of Scots with Mary I.

cs1.tip: Imagine the Crown paid Walsingham's agents through a formal department, not his personal household. Explain two ways the network would change, for better or worse.
cs1.note: A good answer gives two clear changes and says whether each is better or worse. For better, a Crown department would mean steadier funding, so Walsingham would not die in debt. For worse, agents' names could leak to political rivals, putting their cover at risk. A strong answer ties each change to a reason the lesson gives. The trap is listing changes without explaining why they follow from the new system.
